answers.question: I haven't run for two weeks. Do I have to start again from the beginning? And is the 5K in four weeks still realistic?
answers.answer:
No, you do not need to start from the beginning. Pick up at the walk-run level you last finished, 8 runs of 2 minutes each with a 1 minute walk, and build from there. A two-week break is short, so the base from late August should still be there, though the first run back will likely feel harder than the last one did.

Finishing the 5K with walk breaks is realistic in four weeks, and that is a safe goal to keep. Running the whole way is a stretch: it needs continuous running well beyond the 2-minute runs you have done, and beginner plans to reach that usually take well over four weeks. Keep the whole-way target while the runs feel manageable, and be ready to switch to a walk-break finish.

new.analysis:
The week of Oct 12 – 18 had three planned runs, and none of them happened. Nothing was overrun, and the four rest days were taken as planned, so the gap is missed sessions rather than too much running. The week before also had no runs, which is why the gap is two weeks long.

A two-week break is short enough that I am not restarting you from the beginning. Some running fitness will have faded, but the base you built since late August should still be there. Resuming at the level you last finished is the sensible restart.

The stress and short sleep you described are a fair explanation for the gap, and this plan works around them. With about six hours of sleep, the week should stay small: three runs, one faster session, and no jump in volume. Keeping the load low means missed sessions are less likely to pile up again.

Only one session carries faster running, and it sits between an easy run and a rest day. That is the only work at race pace this week, and it is kept short because your base is still thin. Saturday matches the running time you managed before the break, with fewer walk breaks, so the build is gradual.

The heart rate limits sit close to your earlier sessions, which averaged 131 to 143 bpm, so easy should stay easy. The quicker minutes have a cap of 160 bpm, well below your maximum of 182, so you can keep them controlled. I will judge the whole-way goal at your next weekly report, based on whether Saturday feels comfortable and whether the quicker minutes stayed controlled.
